segments.text: Look, we've got
the submissions as read. I don't know if you've
seen the other parties'
submissions as well that we're considering this morning, because there's a bit of a
competition of ideas in there, and we might well ask you questions about what you
think about some of their comments.
But what I'll do is I'll set the time for 10 minutes.
Sure.
And I'll give you a call with four to go if you're still going.
Take the submission as read.
And we do like asking questions, there's probably quite a few.
So, in your hands.
Sure. No problem. Well, thank you, and kia ora tātou. Thank you for having me.
Leonard Samson, Chief Executive of Port of Tauranga.
Look, just
from a port perspective,
Port of Tauranga, we fundamentally oppose extending the Local Government
Informations
Act.
Fundamentally, our view is that the existing commercial accountability
arrangements are fit for purpose, and that the bill would create unnecessary
commercial, legal, and security risks.
The application of the LGOIMA incorrectly treats port companies as
council-controlled organizations when they are commercially
governed businesses.
The purpose of the LGOIMA is to support democratic participation and
accountability in local government objectives, and they do not align
with the port company's commercial mandate.
The commercial mandate of port companies aligns with the Port Companies Act
and it requires ports to operate as successful commercial businesses and provides
accountability measures that are suited to that purpose.
This was a deliberate governance model that Parliament
intentionally created to commercially govern ports and preserve the
agility, confidentiality to promote effective competition in
freight markets.
Another added complexity for Port of Tauranga is that its listed
issuer status as an NZX-listed
company with public and private shareholders, we're already subject to
significant market disclosure and shareholder obligations.
Moving away from the current arrangements would impact
investor confidence. Applying public sector information regimes
could disrupt shareholder relationships, commercial
confidentiality, and investor confidence.
It is also not comparable with other partially publicly owned
businesses operating in competitive markets.
For example, Air New Zealand, Mercury Energy, are not subject to the
comparable official information regimes.
The existing
accountability, reporting, audits, and regulatory oversight and shareholder
scrutiny already provide significant transparency without the need
to extend to further LGOIMA requirements.
And finally, there is no clear or proportionate case.
It's not clear from the bill
that's evidenced any accountability failure, and
it's hard to understand the purposes behind the broad intervention and
disproportionate issue that is claimed.
That's the basis for my submission, so I don't need to take up the full 10 minutes.
I'm happy to take any questions.
Excellent. There's a lot of value in question time. So I'll start with Dan.
Hey, thank you, Leonard. Really good to have your submission and
before our committee today. As a listed
company, I guess there's already a huge amount of
disclosure requirements. Can you kind of elaborate for the
committee
the extent of information requirements that any listed
company has
to the public and to its shareholders?
Fundamentally, there's a continuous disclosure requirement that means anything that
can be considered material, and that material test is
significant. So anything that could be considered to have
a... And it is a test that could have any
influence, whether it be in terms of investor confidence, share
price, et cetera, we need to make disclosures.
So even as simple as
we are employing a new executive team member, we're just about in the process of
looking to make, we need to make that listed issuer disclosure.
Any fundamental changes, any new business
we secure that could be significant to the port and have
an influence
flow through to share price, that needs to require a disclosure.
Any change to governance, any new directors.
So
it's hard to go and list every example because in a lot of cases,
it's pretty much everything anyway.
It's anything that could be considered to be material.
And that material test is not
binary and you err on the side of caution because anything
can be considered material in a lot of cases.
Yeah, thank you. And maybe a second question, if I can, Mr.
Chair, is
as part of your requirements, you run annual general meetings.
I'm assuming they are robust forums
for
your shareholders. Is that correct?
That's correct. We hold
twice
a year interim, so we have an interim and a full year
investor day analyst briefings. And so providing, making sure, and
that's available to all investors.
And so, shareholders have representation at those there.
We also hold annual AGMs, and they are very robust,
with plenty of time for shareholders to go and
participate in terms of questions in advance and
be involved in the governance of the port.
Thank you very much.
Carlos.
Hi. Thank you.
I just wonder if this law is passed, what is the extra or
additional operational cost will it create?
Or how will these changes affect the efficiency and
productivity?
There's a significant impact to--
I guess,
there's a significant administration burden that would be associated with it.
And you would potentially continually be running the test over what's commercially
sensitive and what's not. And so, in a lot of cases when you talk about
from a port company perspective, the model, it
was a deliberate model that was put in place with the Port Companies Act to
actually preserve confidentiality and provide
effective competition within the freight
market. So from
a Legoyma perspective, for example, the international shipping lines, all of those
type of things, you could find yourself being in significant areas where you're
having to redact
a lot of time,
things that could be considered commercially sensitive.
Just the administration function in itself would be a significant burden on
our organization. In terms of impact, in terms of
specifically port productivity, I'm
not sure. And while we support absolute transparency around the
reporting of port productivity figures, this is not the
pathway to do that in terms of the Legoyma pathway.
That is something that there's a separate, as you note here,
Andy. There's a separate piece of work going on in terms
of an inquiry into port company productivity
that should be looking to go and address those type of outcomes.
But the Legoyma requirement won't have any measurable
impact whatsoever in terms of port productivity.
Thank you.
I've got a few questions too. Just first of all, because this comes
out of
the point that you are partially, or all ports are at least partially owned
by-
Yes
... local bodies. The relationship you have with Quayside Holdings,
how could you characterize that? Is it active, passive? What is it?
It's an active relationship. It's a very good relationship.
I guess what I will say here is
the mandate of Quayside, if you like to act as
the custodian or the asset owner of
regional assets,
and with an independent commercial mandate to operate those as
intergenerational investment entities, has effectively acted
as a buffer between
local government, local body politics, if you like, and running a port
operation. Quayside fundamentally make our lives a lot easier
by having an intermediary
in between the Port of Tauranga and the ultimate shareholder
being the regional council. And it allows the Port of Tauranga to focus on
running its business, which is actually running a port operational business and
doing the best we can in terms of providing services to our customers,
and obviously running our business and playing our part in the
community.
No, thanks. Are they subject to Legoyma,
Quayside?
Good question. They will be CCAP potentially.
I'm not entirely sure.
Okay. It'd be good actually if we can understand that because-
I can come back and clarify that for you. Yes.
Yeah, because there are a number of holding companies which hold port assets across
the country, and other assets as well.
Second area of question I just wanted to ask.
In the Port Companies Act, there's the requirement, as you said, and deliberate
requirement of the legislation to act as a successful business, and that is the
only stipulation there. If you look at the definition of
what they usually use definition of successful business, it is not purely
commercial. It's a multiplicity of things which
includes good customer relations, good relations with community,
all that sort of stuff. What's your view of what being a
successful business is and is not?
Well, I think yes,
a successful organization is more than just the commercial
outcomes. But the fact that a commercial is in there, to me
indicates that there needs to be a level of
capital discipline applied to those businesses,
that would be consistent with it being
in a private setting. And I guess what I mean to that, that is one area
that you have the Auditor General as the auditor for the port companies, and
actually holding port companies to account for the capital decisions that they
make. And again, another point I want to raise here,
as
a listed entity is we have those capital disciplines forced upon
us by being a listed entity. We make poor capital decisions, we
see it in our share price the very next day.
We're accountable to our shareholders at any point in time
as and when we make those decisions.
And as I mentioned before, with the
continuous disclosure requirements, any significant capital decisions will
trigger those requirements.
Cool. And look, I wanted to ask one other question because, certainly in our
inquiry and discussions, there is one particular project which you've got on the
go,
which I think we're all vitally interested in, which is the Stella Passage project.
Well, first of all, I'm interested in how you're getting on, but I'm also
interested in how that project would be affected
were it subject to Legoyma.
It's hard to know the nature of the-- It would open up to all
realms of different types of
scrutiny and questioning, and some of which you're going through
a process, whether it be an environmental process and
now in a fast-track panel process that there's a lot of discussions
that are covered under, I guess, in some cases privileged.
So I'm not sure.
But
frankly, I don't think it helps that process at all,
because
I'm not sure what additional transparency you'd have.
Just to answer your first part of your question, which was how are we going in that
process? We just spent three days In a hearing
by the fast-track panel, and
so we await a decision by September.
Excellent. I wish you well.
Thank you.
Thank you. Any other questions, colleagues?
No. Thank you. Look, what I was looking for there was just to understand whether
you thought that would intrude even more into that process.
And look, I will ask tame-
I think inevitably it would do, because you- But without
understanding the nature of the types of
questions that will get asked, inevitably it would.
That would further go and potentially delay it.
I've got a question.
Okay. Tracy's got one other question.
Just because you've raised that.
And then I've got one. Yeah.
It's certainly my understanding that the bill doesn't change any of your
existing reporting obligations.
It just adds something extra. So under the
Auditor-General and the Companies Act, and all of the ways in which you already
assume you have public accountability, do you
have to report on environmental effects, on workplace
practices, on any kind of relationship with public owners?
I say that because I noted that you say that you
describe yourself as
a privately owned business, acknowledging the fact that you are
54% owned by the public essentially.
So
do you already disclose or report on those other factors-
Yes
... or are those the ones-
Yeah, we do. Yeah, absolutely. We disclose annually in our annual
report, we'll always disclose our health and safety metrics. We'll disclose...
We've got extensive environmental metrics that we've developed over the past years.
And again, I guess from our perspective, there are obviously
more and more in terms of ESG requirements, and obviously we're subject to
climate related disclosures
as a listed entity. And so again, that brings a whole another layer of
transparency and reporting requirements that are mandated.
But even in the ones that are not mandated, we already provide all of those in
terms of health and safety,
workplace
reporting. We provide all of that information today and that level of
transparency.
Right. Thank you.
And look, the other question I was going to ask, because it is one that we've
traversed elsewhere, is the issues around transparency of charges.
So whether it's gate charges, port charges, whatever it might be.
We've heard some sort of light touch, com type arrangements,
which some ports essentially say they subject themselves to
already. Have you got a view on how best those charging
regimes might be made as transparent as possible?
Where you would go, where you wouldn't go.
I
guess you go back to the Port Companies Act that requires to operate as a
commercial successful business.
I think if you looked at the port sector across the board, there's not that many
port companies in the entire country that are operating what you would
consider successful commercial businesses.
There are a number of port companies that are operating in negative free cash flow.
So from a
net perspective,
I'm not sure that there's a fundamental issue there.
But port companies, we
have regular
publishing of our tariffs are available on our website.
I'm just not sure in terms of if your question then relates to the
transparency, are they available?
Yes, they're publicly available
at any point in time, but there's always a process that you go through with our
customers in those discussions, and I suspect each port
company as
its own business needs to go and undertake those processes.
Yeah. Okay. No, that's really helpful. Thank you, Leonard.
Really appreciate the time. Really appreciate the submission and wish you well for
September.
Thank you very much. Thank you for having me.
Thanks, Leonard. Thank you.
Cheers. Bye.

Morning Clint, Carl, and Rob.
Morning.

Yeah, as you say, our submission speaks for itself and,

I'll hand it over to Rob and Clint to go through it in a bit more finer

Thank you, Carl.
So our view is that ports are strategic national assets.
But despite being fully or partially
council owned and key nodes in our transport network, there is
input from the normal transparency that applies to other strategic transport assets
like NZTA.
Even privately owned asset holders like electricity lines companies and airports
are subject to more oversight through the Commerce Commission that doesn't apply to
seaports.
Responding to some of the issues raised by the previous
submitter,
not all ports are listed on the NZX, and the
transparency requirements of the NZX are fundamentally different from
official information legislation.
As he himself alluded to,
with his
claims that
complying with official information disclosure would be burdensome.
Now, responding to that point, I'm a school board chair.
We're a small school. We are subject to disclosure under
the Official Information Act. We have to do that.
If a small school can manage it, I think a large port can.
The costs are relatively minor and transparency is important.
The issues with the The lack of transparency in the current regime was exemplified
by Ports of Auckland's lack of transparency during the 2012
lockout and during their disastrous automation project.
This bill is timely
because as the committee has recently heard during the ports inquiry, New Zealand
is moving towards a hub and spoke model port organization where
international vessels will service only a few key ports and freight
will be transported between those ports and regional spokes by coastal vessels.
That is going to happen whether it is a government-led process or imposed
on us by international shipping lines.
A hub and spoke model to be successful for New Zealand will require a national
port strategy and greater coordination of investment between
ports and
with government to ensure we have the infrastructure where we need it
and that we need. That won't be possible if ports continue to act as
if they're simple, private, isolated identities like the corner shop
rather than the strategic assets in our transport network that they are.
So this bill will help put New Zealand in a better place
for the reality that we are facing in the port sector as we move
towards a hub and spoke model.
The one
amendment that MANZ has suggested would be to ensure that private
operators are also covered by the disclosure regime.
The prospect of privatization of port operations, as is currently being
proposed for Lyttelton, should not become a loophole to avoid
transparency and stymie coordination.
And
we see that being a real risk
that
the transparency that's needed and that this bill would help to
accomplish
would be stymied if we see private operators exempted from it.
Thank you.
Thank you.
You good for questions?
Yes.
Okay, cool. Right. Questions, colleagues. Tracy.
Thanks.
Thank you, and thank you for your submission.
Can you give me some examples of what sort of specific information
that you've been unable to
obtain from ports that you
would have liked to have?
Well, the Ports of Auckland automation process was
a huge example of where hundreds of millions of dollars of
what was ultimately ratepayers' money was wasted by port
management who had this--
They wanted to de-unionize the port, and they
had this vainglorious idea of themselves.
During that process,
the union was largely shut out.
De-unionizing the port was part of the goal of the automation process, and
councilors also found it hard to get information out of the port what was
happening. Our belief is that if there had been greater
transparency during that automation process, then the alarm
bells would've been able to be sounded much earlier, before all that money was
wasted, before
the lives of workers were lost.
Yeah. I've got an example of actually being at a hearing with the council,
where elected councilors were asking the
CEO
at the time, during the dispute in 2012,
some questions, and he just kept hiding behind the corporate veil, saying it was
sensitive information
that he couldn't share because it had implications to the
company. And
as we all know the result of what that carry on
did to
the port.
And so
it really has to stop, this covering up and hiding behind
that corporate veil. The
community should be able to ask questions and get straight
answers.
There's got to be some accountability. That's what we're after.
And I don't think it's necessarily just the community either in discussions.
We talked about this during the ports inquiry and discussions we had with the
Infrastructure Commission last year.
They also described difficulty mapping in terms of
getting the information to map what is effectively incredibly vital infrastructure.
So
that speaks to the need to plan and,
as Clint said, the fact that lack of transparency stymies the ability to
plan at a national level.
Yeah.
Can I ask two questions? The first one of them is, the Port of Auckland, obviously,
who you focused on, because I know obviously the history there,
is not subject to the same kind of disciplines that the NZX were put on
that
Port Taranaki was just talking about.
If the same discipline were required, anything that's commercially
significant and obviously the investment that was being made and
the automation would've absolutely been in that category, so would any risks to
that associated with that. That would make that actually
ironically more transparent than it was
by the looks of it. Would that be fair?
I'm not advocating for a second for
privatization, but what I am wondering aloud about is whether in fact
if that same discipline was there for the non-privatized,
the fully publicly owned companies, whether that would actually make a difference.
Well, obviously there is greater transparency, but it's a particular kind of
transparency.
This
bill would allow
greater discourse, greater inquiry.
We don't see that the disclosures that you get on
the NZX are necessarily
completely aligned with the disclosure that you would need, for instance,
in making a national assessment across all ports.
It is better, but it's not
necessarily fit for purpose. It's a sort of halfway measure or
a tool with a different purpose.
And that takes me to the other question I was going to ask, which is, we've
certainly had quite a number of conversations around the port
inquiry, which have gone to the transparency for things like charging
regimes, et cetera, investment regimes and so on.
Whether the Commerce Commission has a light touch or a heavier touch
oversight of ports is, I think, a live question that's been
raised with us.
What it seems is that the LGOIMA, I'm well aware of from a local government point
of view, is exceedingly intrusive.
Possibly more than anybody actually realizes who's made submissions, because I've
been on the other end of it, I know how intrusive it is.
But at the moment we've got
such a light touch, in your view anyway, that you're not getting the information
that's needed. Is there a halfway house, I guess is what I'm
asking you.
And it may be through a range of different pieces of legislation.
Yeah. You're right that the Commerce
Commission, if they had powers over the seaports, could
require disclosure of information that's not publicly disclosable now.
That's not the question that's in front of us.
Right.
We see that there'll be real benefits to this, particularly as we move towards the

Okay, cool. Julianne. Oh, sorry.

It's not open slather.
Yeah. I know how it works.
Julianne.

understandable that they're defending their position to not have to comply with

Yeah. I'd say that the port's position is not surprising,
that they'd be opposed to greater transparency.
I think as the previous submitter showed, the
ethos of the ports tends to be that they're just private companies, just
the same as the corner dairy, the same as a factory making widgets.
Our view is that
they are not. They are strategic assets that all of
them have some level of public ownership, and they are vital to New
Zealand's economic future.
We are
moving towards this hub and spoke model, and they
are each crucial nodes in that hub and spoke, whether
they'll be spokes or hubs. So,
in our view, transparency is vital.
But it's not surprising that
their view accords to how they view themselves.
Cool. Look, thank you very much. Really appreciate it, and also really appreciate

It's been most helpful to get all the input we've had.
Thank you.
Thank you very much.
Thanks, man.

Good morning.

You've got 10 minutes. I'll give you a call with four to go,

And so, in your hands.
Very good. Well, thank you very much.
Tēnā koutou katoa, and thank you for the opportunity to speak to
the select committee on our submission
on the Local Government Ports Accountability Bill.
I'm Melissa Ransom-Bridges. I'm the Secretary of the New Zealand Council of Trade
Unions, and joining me is Corey Bourne, who is in our
policy team as a senior policy advisor.
We represent over 32 affiliated unions, including
MUNZ, who you just heard from. And also,
the RMTU, who I understand has also submitted on this bill.
And just to start off, we'd like to begin by saying that we endorse and
support the points made in their submissions.
Collectively, we represent over 370,000
working people across Aotearoa, New Zealand.
And we also acknowledge Te Tiriti o Waitangi as the founding document of
Aotearoa, and represent over 60,000 kaimahi
Maori through our affiliated unions as well.
So we support this bill. We see it as
a modest and practical and also an important
step to bring port companies into the same accountability
framework as other council-controlled organizations.
Ports are publicly owned and publicly connected
critical infrastructure, and decisions about them can have
major consequences for workers, for local
communities, for regional economies, supply
chains, iwi and hapū, and also for the
environment. These decisions should therefore be
made with appropriate transparency, accountability, and
also, importantly for us, regard to good employment practice.
We consider that this bill helps achieve that without
undermining any commercial role of port companies.
I'm going to hand over now to Corey to go through our submission
in a bit more detail. And also obviously for
even more detail, we defer to MUNZ and RMTU, who have a
particularly
good understanding of the issues at play in this legislation. Thank you.
Now, Kia ora, select committee . As Mel opened with, the
accountability and transparency critical to port companies' social license to
operate. They operate and occupy significant public
infrastructure on public land, public assets, and they are delivering
essential services.
I'm sure you'll probably hear this a lot today, but we know that 99% of the
country's international trade by volume comes through our ports.
So we're not here to dispute that they're not cr-- they are critical
infrastructure, both regionally and nationally.
The scale and impact of their operations are very diverse.
So they're large employers in their local communities.
And with port land use on the waterfront, it means there are relevant environmental
and cultural factors, and therefore a number of different interests in the
governance of these assets.
We think the bill introduces some fairly minor changes that will help with the
accountability to those local interests, and note that submission of
demands around ensuring that those privately operated
ports aren't
out of scope of those provisions, too.
We would suggest that this bill isn't creating new obligations out of nowhere,
applies those existing understood rules from the
LGOIMA that other entities already work
within. We're not looking at special treatment for
the ports, just to remove that historical exemption that's seen them left out.
And as we heard from Munz, that there is those withholding grounds built
in. Andy, you were saying that you feel like it is quite
intrusive, but there are grounds there around withholding information and
if there's
too much to disclose, those protections are there, we would
suggest.
Secondly, just want to talk briefly to the importance of supporting good work that
this bill seeks to do. Unsurprisingly, we're widely focused
on supporting good work, which is mahi that has a lasting positive
impact on the worker, the employer, the wider community.
Good work means, among other things, fair wages, health and safe work,
productive and cooperative workplaces, and meaningful and fulfilling work that
contributes to society.
We are therefore supportive of this bill to help port companies and their
workforces realize good work.
They're more and more understanding these days that businesses operate beyond a
narrow view of profit margins and the operations impact the workforces and the
communities that they are based in.
Again, suggesting that this bill is just bringing ports into that already
established framework and not trying to overhaul the regulatory framework around
them, but support them to be locally beneficial and accountable
operations. My background's health and safety, so I'm going to focus on
that as one aspect of good work. Port work is
physically demanding, it's high risk, often involves shift work and other forms
of work like that. It means that we
see some serious health and safety issues, fatigue, moving plant and
vehicles, rail operations, working at heights, among others.
These have fatal consequences if governance is poor.
Alongside worker engagement, good governance is the critical
element of successful workplace health and safety.
In our written sub, we highlighted the turnaround of the operations at Ports of
Auckland as something that regulatory settings should support.
Ports of Auckland had that horrendous health and safety record with some severe
failings that led to worker fatalities and then first HSWA
conviction of an officer.
But that turnaround, that was bringing good governance and the workforce of Ports
of Auckland together and saw the port significantly increase its
productivity,
and at the same time dramatically increasing employee engagement.
So we think those are the kind of settings that regulatory settings should try and
support and practice. And while the bill, we say it's only light touch, but we
think it will slightly move the needle in that way.
And just want to make the final point that good employment is not in competition
with commercial performance. In fact, it's the opposite that's often
true, where productive businesses are those that work with their employees, they're
safe, and they are productive.
Beyond the employment sphere,
we think it's important for ports to demonstrate social and environmental
responsibility by having regard to the interests of the community in which they
operate.
We think regulatory settings should support the ports to work
with their workforce, their local communities, including iwi and hapū, to
mitigate their impacts on the environment and continue to maintain their social
license to operate. On that basis, we recommend that-
We've got about three and a half minutes left.
Just finishing. Final sentence.
Oh
We are recommending that the bill
passes for that balanced approach to transparency and accountability of these
critical assets and for supporting the ports to be good employers for everyone's
benefit. Thank you for your time.
Thank you both. Colleagues, looking for questions. Tracy.
Thank you.

examples of how having
better direct access to information around health and safety

But to the point around information sharing, that is a critical element of

When you're engaging the workers and they need to
know what the
decision-making processes are, what the issues are that we're actually trying to
address. So having as much information as possible is helpful
when you're collaborating on health and safety responses to things
on the ports.
Okay, thank you.
Two questions from me, if I can.
First one of them is, you've talked about in your written
submission
that at, two, the profit margins are the sole
concern.
Now, I note that the Port
Companies Act actually says operate a successful business.
Yeah.
As I understand, there is no legal Definition of successful business, but

it's natural for monopolies to continually increase prices and adopt a cost

charges being

There's a contagion effect of new charges across ports.

in
smart flow fees from forestry with no demonstrable improvement in service

Yes.

Thank you.
